source.title: PrisonBreak: Jailbreaking Large Language Models with Fewer Than Twenty-Five Targeted Bit-flips
source.authors: Zachary Coalson; Jeonghyun Woo; Chris S. Lin; Joyce Qu; Yu Sun; Shi-Yang Chen; Lishan Yang; Gururaj Saileshwar; Prashant J. Nair; Bo Fang; Sanghyun Hong

record.file_problem: None apparent; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper applies the refusal-direction ablation as a comparator and measures refusal-direction expression during its own bit-flip attack. It argues, based on its results, that the bit-flip attack can reduce refusal without suppressing that direction, refining the claim that jailbreaks work by suppressing it.
record.gate_note: The paper computes the harmful-minus-benign activation direction and reports a cosine-similarity comparison across attacks. It also evaluates Ortho, which it describes as estimating and ablating the refusal direction, and reports Ortho's harmful-response rates and utility changes. Values used only to select attack parameters or search settings are not recorded as results. The UMAP activation visualizations are not rows because they do not directly measure the refusal direction or refusal rate.
record.test_reason: The paper runs refusal-direction ablation (Ortho, Arditi et al.'s weight-orthogonalized form) on 10 models, reporting HarmBench ASR and TinyBenchmarks utility. It also measures cosine similarity to the diff-in-means direction under GCG and under its own bit-flip jailbreak. It reports that the bit-flip attack jailbreaks without suppressing the direction, which bears on V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that PrisonBreak jailbreaks with 5–25 bit-flips while preserving utility, and that it works differently from GCG and Ortho: refusal-direction expression stays close to the clean model, so the attack may instead amplify activations associated with responding.
record.recipe_differences: The study's own intervention is targeted weight bit-flipping, not the difference-in-means direction ablation. It also evaluates Ortho as a comparator, but does not test adding the direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported directional behavior differs by attack method: Ortho has zero cosine similarity, GCG shows less agreement, and PrisonBreak remains close to clean. Ortho's harmful-response rate also varies across models.

fits_no_version.finding: Models with more post-training alignment (RLHF/DPO) need more bit-flips (13–25 vs 5–20) to jailbreak.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment method affects robustness of refusal to sparse weight corruption.

record.problems: Directional cosine results are presented in a plot without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The Ortho harmful-response rates do not reach complete refusal removal on all tested models. Capability is assessed using TINY BENCHMARKS accuracy; the paper does not report uncertainty for those measurements.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results on the claim's direction or its refusal behavior were left out.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal; per-layer or per-position ablation details; capability beyond TinyBenchmarks.
Ortho is run by the authors on open models; publicly released abliterated checkpoints are not evaluated.
Training against refusal-direction ablation for robustness; prompt jailbreaks other than GCG.

missing.what: UMAP of last-layer activations: under Ortho, harmful-prompt activations move near benign ones; under PrisonBreak, harmful activations stay a separate cluster. Qualitative and figure-only.
missing.locator: Figure 4 middle/right, Section 8.2, Appendix D Figure 5 (Qwen2-7B)

record.verdict_notes: Ortho is a baseline that the authors tuned for maximum ASR. ASR comes from the HarmBench classifier, and the authors note this classifier can overcount degenerate outputs. The V3 evidence rests on a single model (Vicuna-13B), figure-only, with no numbers. The bit-flip attack is a weight-level attack rather than a prompt jailbreak, hence limits_scope rather than challenges.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test adding the direction. It does not establish that the direction is ablated at every layer and position, or report an independent test of general capability beyond the benchmark accuracy used for Ortho.
The paper tests bit-flip attacks on weights, not a weight edit that converts the refusal-direction ablation into an abliteration.
The paper does not test training against refusal-direction ablation as a robustness method.
No test of affine, cone-shaped, or multiple-direction accounts of refusal is reported.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision is reported.
The reported transfer is of bit-flip locations, not of the refusal direction.
The paper compares bit-flip susceptibility across models with different alignment training, but does not test whether training determines whether a removable refusal direction exists.

relation.reason: The paper runs Ortho itself on 10 models, with untreated baselines and a capability check, and measures direction expression under its attacks.

tranche.reason: Ortho is only partial on three models. The authors also state explicitly that PrisonBreak jailbreaks without suppressing the refusal direction, which means V3 needs restating.

source_check.notes: The text is arXiv v3, titled 'With at Most Twenty-Five Targeted Bit-flips' (the pack's title differs). Ortho is a comparator: the paper gives no implementation details (layer, direction selection, code). ASR is the HarmBench classifier's harmful rate, not a refusal rate. The cosine analysis covers Vicuna-13B-v1.5 only and is figure only.

statements.correction: 2412.07192: Ortho on ten models (Vicuna-7B-v1.3/v1.5, Vicuna-13B-v1.5, Llama 2-7B/13B, Llama 3-8B/70B, Tulu 3-8B, Qwen 2-1.5B/7B). HarmBench ASR goes from 1.26–18.24% to 56.60–93.71%. The four named values are correct (rows r4, r6, r7, r10). Hyperparameters searched for highest ASR; HarmBench classifier.
statements.problem: The 'why' says 2412.07192 is 'on nine models', but Ortho is run on ten. The cited rows (r1,r3,r4,r6,r7,r11) don't match the four models named (r4,r6,r7,r10), and r11 holds a wrong value.

statements.correction: 2412.07192: Ortho hyperparameters searched for highest ASR. HarmBench classifier, default HF chat template. ASR 3.14→56.60 (Llama 2-13B), 18.24→67.30 (Vicuna-7B-v1.5), 9.43→71.70 (Qwen 2-1.5B), so 28–43% of 159 prompts not judged harmful.
statements.problem: The conditions call the edits 'standard (non-searched)', but this study ran an extensive hyperparameter search for Ortho. 'Keep most refusal' also overstates for this study: most responses are judged harmful.

statements.correction: 2412.07192, Llama 2-7B, Ortho: HarmBench ASR 1.26%→84.91% (r4). System prompt not stated; 'default chat template' from HF model cards.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but the row cited is r7, which in this record is Llama 3-70B (8.18→93.71). The Llama 2-7B row is r4.

statements.correction: 2412.07192, ten models: no-attack ASR 1.26–18.24% → Ortho 56.60–93.71%. Seven models are at 81.13–93.71%. The other three: Llama 2-13B 56.60%, Vicuna-7B-v1.5 67.30%, Qwen 2-1.5B 71.70%.
statements.problem: 'Ten models, ASR 1.26-13.84% -> 81.76-93.71%' is wrong. Across the ten models the ranges are wider, and even the seven-model high group starts at 81.13%.

statements.correction: 2412.07192: on Vicuna-13B-v1.5, GCG-M lowers the cosine similarity of HarmBench last-token activations to the diff-in-means direction, relative to the clean model (Fig. 4 left, figure only, correlational).
statements.problem: Cites r22, but the 'what' and 'why' never name this study or say what it found.

statements.correction: 2412.07192: PrisonBreak on Vicuna-13B-v1.5 reaches 90.57% ASR, with cosine close to the clean model (figure only).
statements.problem: The model is not named. 90.57% is the Vicuna-13B-v1.5 value; the average over the ten models is 89.56%.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Ortho's direction ablation yields 93.08% and 93.71% harmful-response rates, respectively, with small reported benchmark changes; see r6, r7, r16, r17.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The ablation's harmful-response rates vary from 56.60% to 84.91%, so refusal is not uniformly removed; see r1-r5 and r8-r10.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Ortho eliminates directional agreement and GCG has reduced agreement with the refusal direction; see r21-r22.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: PrisonBreak has a 90.57% harmful-response rate while directional agreement remains close to clean, countering the claim that this attack works by suppressing the direction; see r23-r24.
